title: Lift yourself
hookLine: let a person lift the self by the self; the self is its own friend and enemy (Bhagavad Gita 6.5)
tomorrow: why does a god on a battlefield care how high your seat is?

lines: THE OFFER LANDS. THE STOMACH DROPS.
cards: Good news can land like bad news: the offer arrives, suddenly it's real, and the stomach drops. The first chapter of the Bhagavad Gita builds to a man in a far heavier version of that spot.
Two armies face each other on the field of Kurukshetra. The conch shells have sounded.
Arjuna, the archer, asks his charioteer Krishna to drive him out between the lines, and he looks across: teachers, uncles, cousins, friends. His limbs give way. His mouth goes dry.
His bow, Gandiva, slips from his hand. And then he sits down in the chariot and lets the bow and arrows go.

teach.h: A MAN WHO HAS SAT DOWN.
teach.b: That's where Arjuna's lesson starts: not with a hero, but with a man who has sat down. Krishna's first answer is sharp: shake off this weakness, and stand. It doesn't work.
So the talk goes long, and by the sixth chapter Krishna gives the answer from the inside.

teach.h: LIFT THE SELF BY THE SELF.
teach.b: Let a person lift the self by the self, and not let the self sink. The self alone is its own friend; the self alone is its own enemy.
The next verse turns it: the self is a friend to the one who has mastered it, and an enemy to the one who hasn't.

A detail worth passing on: in the Sanskrit, the same word, atman, the self, sits on both sides of the sentence: the one who lifts and the one who's lifted. So in the Gita, being your own friend isn't a pep talk or a mood.
It's yoga: a mind trained by its own practice, until the trained part can carry the shaky part. That's why this chapter goes straight on to practice.
The Gita doesn't leave everything to effort; later chapters speak of devotion and grace.
But this verse is plain. Krishna can drive the chariot and teach. Arjuna has to stand up.

how: The Bhagavad Gita is part of the Mahabharata; Hindus study, recite and teach it, and verse 6.5, lift the self by the self, belongs to its chapter on meditation.

o: praising yourself out loud until the doubt goes away
raising your own self by your own steady practice
waiting for a teacher to pull you out of a slump

games.q: who's who on the chariot: tap the pairs.
p: the bow that slips from his hand
the self: both lifter and lifted

s: in the Gita, 'be your own friend' means simply feel good about yourself
the next verse says the self is a friend to the one who has mastered it: friendship through practice.
before the battle, Arjuna's bow slips from his hand
in chapter one his limbs give way, his mouth goes dry, and Gandiva slips.
in the Gita, Krishna does Arjuna's rising for him
Krishna drives and teaches. the verse says the self lifts the self.

games.q: you're handed a big new task and a voice in your head says you'll fail. in the Gita's terms, what's the friend move?
o: take the next practiced step; the trained self carries the shaky one.
wait until you feel confident; the friend shows up as a feeling.
hand it to someone stronger; Krishna lifts Arjuna, so others lift you.
games.why: in Gita 6.5–6 the self lifts the self, and it's a friend once it's mastered. a practice, not a mood.

practice: Find a pen and something to write on. Write one hard thing you're facing, and under it, the sentence the steady, practiced part of you would say about it: not flattery, the true thing. Read it back once, slowly, in your own voice.

wordCard.voice: Lift yourself: the Gita's line that the self raises the self, and is a friend to the one who has trained it.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Bhagavad Gita 6.5: let one lift the self by the self. atman is on both sides.

carryVoice: Keep this one: my own friend, the part of me that practices. Four days into the Gita.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 1.28–30, 1.47 (Arjuna's limbs give way, Gandiva slips from his hand, he sits down in the chariot and casts aside bow and arrows)
Bhagavad Gita 2.3 (Krishna: cast off this weakness and arise)
Bhagavad Gita 6.5–6 (lift the self by the self; the self is its own friend and enemy; a friend to the one who has conquered it)
